item.title: Understanding Autism in Women: 3 Support Strategies Beyond Medication
item.description:
For years, she thought she was simply “too sensitive.” Crowded stores felt exhausting. Bright lights were distracting. Conversations in groups felt overwhelming, and she often replayed them in her mind afterward, wondering if she had said the wrong thing. Many women spend years believing they are shy, anxious, or “too much,” only to discover later in life that Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) may help explain experiences they have had since childhood.

Autism in women is often diagnosed at a much later age because the signs are either missed or diagnosed under different ailments (1). But when a woman does receive a diagnosis of ASD, there is promising research for treatments that do not rely as heavily on medication.

What Is Autism Spectrum Disorder?

ASD is a developmental, neurodivergent condition that involves significant challenges in communication and social interaction, as well as limitations in behavior patterns. This includes repetitive, highly limited or restricted interests, and inflexibility, among others. The DSM-5 diagnostic criteria were updated by the American Psychiatric Association in 2022.

If you think you or a loved one may have ASD but have yet to be diagnosed, we recommend seeing a licensed therapist in one of our offices to discuss your concerns.

Why Autism in Women Gets Missed

There are several reasons a girl may be categorized as “normal” or as having a shy personality or possibly diagnosed with anxiety instead of autism when she’s growing up.

One reason is that anyone — female or male — who is naturally less expressive will not exhibit the expressive signs of another more overt personality who is struggling with social interaction. Another reason is that some of the research used to set the gold standard of autism measures was set using boys as the model, and girls present differently (1).

While a boy with autism may be flagged for an evaluation because he limits his toys to dinosaurs and stacks them repeatedly, a girl may not be flagged because she is playing with her dolls. However, what a teacher or parent might not notice is that within her pretend play, the girl is also exhibiting behavioral patterns that would signify the need for further assessment.

A girl may play by lining up the dolls and mimicking the same pretend story over and over. The reason the girl did not get assessed in the first place is that her play traits are more characteristic of her gender than the boy’s, and they are less noticeable.

Autism in women also gets missed because they learn to cope by masking their neurodivergent patterns of behavior and mimicking the behaviors they see of normalized social cues. This can be exhausting, and it often leads to burnout (2). For many women, masking becomes so automatic that they do not realize how much energy it requires until they begin experiencing chronic exhaustion or burnout. Many women do not seek treatment until they recognize the signs of burnout and wonder what could be causing their extreme responses to what appear to be everyday social interactions.

What Might Autism in Women Look Like?

Women with autism have similar interests to any woman, but some of the neurodivergences can include:

● Preferring one-on-one discussions instead of group discussions
● Sensory avoidance and sensitivity to light or sound
● Internalizing shutdowns so they appear to be zoning out, but in actuality, they are overwhelmed by external stimuli
● Practicing scripts to mimic the social norms that are expected
● Adopting personas to become like what they think they should be, e.g., an organized student or a helpful co-worker
● Stemming behaviors that aren’t as overt, such as hair twirling, cuticle picking, or quiet humming
● Misunderstanding conflicts, particularly in relationships or friendships
● Inability to maintain long-term friendships due to frustration, inflexibility, or limited interests

While every person is different, autism in women can also appear differently because there are levels of autism. These are some of the characteristics that might help you or someone you love find something relatable and a reason to reach out.

Treatments for Autism in Women Beyond Medicine

While medicines can provide relief to specific symptoms, this article maintains that a licensed counselor will work with a woman to determine those. It is important not to self-diagnose. Some women will have other conditions alongside ASD, and it is essential to understand their entire mental health portfolio to manage all conditions together.

Recent research suggests that a promising discovery could be beneficial, particularly for women (3) who struggle with sensory challenges related to autism. Using VR technology, one small study noted that women were better able to self-regulate when they were overstimulated. The technology allowed them to choose their own room filled with silence, and it did not matter what their physical location was.

This game-changer could be pivotal in helping anyone with autism, particularly in areas where moving locations is not an option, such as traveling through airports or in shopping malls. The research and prototype are still in their early stages, but the findings are promising.

Other treatments include resource-based support, such as guiding adolescents into adulthood by helping them with life skills and communication. An Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) support can help adolescents transition through coaching that’s targeted to their specific needs.

The ABA might include breaking down large skill sets into smaller chunks for practical problem-solving. Practical examples are using ABA to ensure you are getting on the right bus at the end of your shift, or how to answer questions appropriately in a job interview.

Self-assessment and reflection tools also help autistic adults as they learn how to identify their own skill gaps. Then, they can recognize what guidance could be helpful as they seek treatment from a therapist. Reflecting on how they feel in relationships, friendships, or the workplace may help reveal a particular challenge with interpersonal communication.

On the other hand, a guided tool geared toward women with autism may ask about self-care habits, such as sleep, hobbies, and routines. These questions can provide clues related to a need for more attention to broadening interests or expanding routines.

Vocation and social support are also shown to be effective. Especially for autism in women, you or your loved one may have wondered why a specific line of work has been so challenging, and the diagnosis may shed some light on it.

With vocational support and the Americans with Disabilities Act, several companies are designing inclusive workspaces, programs, and workplace roles that enable a person diagnosed with ASD to thrive. Social support may include one-on-one peer feedback or group therapy, both guided by licensed therapists.

Research on Autism in Women

While the research on autism in women is still emerging, the future of support, treatment, and vitality is strong. Several universities have developed programs of study for adult learners with autism, recognizing the need for further advancement.

One recent study showed that clinicians need to keep autism on their radar when women seek treatment for other conditions, such as eating disorders, anxiety, burnout, and ADHD. Some women may have comorbidities or have been misdiagnosed at the time they initially sought treatment.

Next Steps

If you suspect that you or another adult woman you know has autism, there are a few ways you can help. Depending on the nature of your relationship, you can consider the following:

· When was the most recent appointment with her primary care physician?
· What other challenges are present?
· What are some of the past obstacles socially, academically, and interpersonally?

After that, or if you are the person you suspect may be autistic, you can contact a licensed psychologist or psychiatrist who specializes in ASD. Our offices are staffed with therapists who have the appropriate training and experience to help you on your journey to thriving and well-being.

One thing to keep in mind is that there is not one test or assessment that clinicians use to decide if you have autism. Instead, the diagnosis will be based on a variety of questionnaires, your medical and health history, and you will likely need multiple appointments. But the important part is that you will have access to support once you are diagnosed — whether you have autism or not.

Take the first step and reach out for an initial evaluation. In the meantime, you can read articles about autism spectrum disorder and watch videos of other adults who were diagnosed later in life. It may encourage you to hear about their stories, so you will be informed, educated, and motivated for the path ahead.

Autism in women is often more complex to assess than in men, especially during childhood and adolescence. If you relate to anything you’ve read here, it is wise to seek an expert opinion. Contact an office near you today.

References
1. Dolfi, A., & Tudose, C. (2025). Diagnostic challenges of autism spectrum disorder in women without intellectual or language impairments: a narrative review. Journal of Medicine and Life, 18(8), 710.
2. Gonçalves Garcia, S., da Silveira Simões-Pires, C., Acosta Brum, J., & Centurion Cabral, J. (2026). Taking off the mask: Investigating autism diagnosis and camouflaging in adult women. Autism in Adulthood, 8(4), 677-686.
3. Leonardi, S., Di Cara, M., Giliberto, S., Piccolo, A., De Domenico, C., Leonardi, G., … & Cucinotta, F. (2025). The use of multisensory environments in children and adults with autism spectrum disorder: A systematic review. Autism, 29(8), 1921-1938.

item.title: Understanding and Finding Healing from Intergenerational Trauma
item.description:
Can we ever truly escape the past? Sometimes it can feel as though the past repeats itself, and its chains have us in an iron grip we cannot release ourselves from.

It can be daunting to look at your own past and see the ways it reaches into your present. Wounds from the past, such as intergenerational trauma, can influence your day-to-day patterns and behavior. The good news is that the future is an open vista, and lasting healing is a real possibility.

Intergenerational Trauma: What Is It?

When we think about trauma, we often think about painful or distressing experiences that happen directly to us. Intergenerational trauma, however, refers to the ways the effects of trauma can continue beyond the generation that originally experienced it. Unresolved emotional wounds, learned beliefs, unhealthy coping strategies, relationship patterns, and responses to fear or stress can influence children and later generations, even when they did not experience the original traumatic event themselves.

Intergenerational trauma can occur within families or entire communities and may be passed down in subtle as well as more obvious ways. Over time, these patterns can affect a person’s emotional well-being, relationships, behaviors, and even how they understand themselves and the world around them.

People experiencing intergenerational trauma may struggle with forming healthy relationships, unexplained depression or anxiety, patterns of self-sabotage or fear, or a sense of carrying a burden they struggle to name. These effects can occur in the present even when the original painful or traumatic events happened decades or generations before.

Some Examples of Intergenerational Trauma in Scripture

While the term ‘intergenerational trauma’ is something that has gained currency in recent decades, that does not mean that the reality it names is new. Scripture is quite candid about how sin has consequences; our brokenness and the brokenness of others that we endure, and experience all have consequences, and these can ripple through generations.

Two examples of this can help us. One is to consider the family of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, which we read about from Genesis 12 until the end of the book. In story after story, there are repeated patterns of deeply damaging favoritism, selfishness, and deception, which cause ongoing conflict and shape the dynamics in the family across generations. In Jacob’s story, in particular, the threat of violence looms as he interacts with his brother Esau and his uncle, Laban.

Another example is David, a great king, warrior, and a man with many moral failings. After committing adultery with Bathsheba and arranging to have her husband killed, the Lord warned David that his actions would have lasting consequences in his own family (2 Samuel 11-12). David’s own son sexually assaulted his half-sister, and David did nothing about it. As a result, his family experienced even more violence and betrayal through revenge and a violent civil war.

The cycles of violence, betrayal, deception, and more that affected these families are tied to longstanding patterns of behavior that are rooted even further in the past. While this is true, Scripture also tells us that there is hope in the Lord to break such cycles.

There is the possibility of redemption, restoration, and a brand-new story for those who seek Him and pursue the new life that is possible in Him (Romans 8; 2 Corinthians 5:17).

The Causes and Triggers of Intergenerational Trauma

From what is known, intergenerational trauma has its roots in a traumatic experience a person, family, or community has. A significant event, unresolved pain, or prolonged suffering can be at the root of what goes on to become intergenerational trauma. These events could include abuse, abandonment or loss, poverty, war, forced migration, and familial patterns of violence or addiction.

These various events and experiences operate on several levels. Some of them, like experiences of war, genocide, or forced migration and displacement, are collective events that scar entire communities. Facing systemic oppression and stress from poverty and discrimination can also affect a community that is the target of such measures. There are also family dysfunctions, such as abuse, addiction, neglect, or abandonment, that can become normalized over time in a family unit.

Future generations within a community or family may not experience the original traumatic event. Still, they may inherit emotional and behavioral patterns that were formed as a response to the pain. These patterns would include anxious attachment, aggression, or deep mistrust.

Intergenerational trauma and its effects may become more noticeable during times of stress or transition. These experiences can activate learned emotional and behavioral patterns, attachment wounds, and stress responses that have been shaped by family experiences across generations.

For example, getting married or becoming a parent can trigger unresolved attachment wounds from one’s childhood or resurface old family patterns.

Other situations that may trigger this trauma include conflict situations and situations of loss and injustice that mirror those of past generations. Such conflict situations may trigger inherited anger or fears. Witnessing violence in one’s community or going through financial hardship can also activate a heightened stress response that affects one’s physical and mental well-being.

Some Signs of Intergenerational Trauma to Look Out for

Intergenerational trauma can manifest in various ways. Often, it escapes detection because it can appear as normal, and just the way your family or community does things. To pick up on how certain patterns are rooted in trauma and anything but ‘normal’ requires close examination and the willingness to make changes toward a healthier outlook. Some signs to look out for include the following:

Hypervigilance This is when you are constantly on edge, and you feel unsafe even in safe spaces.

Unhealthy relationship patterns This includes patterns of shame, denial, secrecy, mistrust, and recurring patterns of codependency.

Relational breakdown Patterns of repeated relational breakdowns across generations within the family may also point to intergenerational trauma.

Emotional problems Issues with regulating moods and emotions, persistent anxiety, depression, or emotional numbness may suggest intergenerational trauma. Also, having emotional overreactions to seemingly unrelated events could be the result of reacting to past traumas.

Inherited beliefs Carrying certain unstated or unconscious beliefs that shape your self-understanding could be a sign of intergenerational trauma. These beliefs could include feeling you are not worthy or that the world is a dangerous place. Persistent feelings of guilt or worthlessness without a clear cause may suggest intergenerational trauma.

Physical symptoms These would include insomnia, chronic pain, or stress-related conditions like heart disease.

A list of possible symptoms is a first step to help you identify what you or a loved one may be experiencing. However, various physical, emotional, and mental health challenges carry similar symptoms, and that is why it’s important to see a health professional. They can help you eliminate possible causes so that you can identify the root cause and address it.

Finding Healing from Intergenerational Trauma

This article started by posing a question – can we ever truly escape the past? Your past is your past, and you cannot change it. However, there is always hope for your future to look different, and to lessen the hold of the past on the here and now. There is freedom in Christ (Galatians 5:1), and with help, you can confront the past to step into a new chapter for you and your loved ones.

“So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.” John 8:36 ESV

The path to hope and a new future may include the following:

Acknowledge the pain Healing comes when you identify that there is a problem, a set of patterns of behaviors that are undermining the fullness of life the Lord intends for you. Reflect on your family history, naming the patterns there and recognizing how they have shaped you.

Seek the Lord’s healing You can do this through prayer, reading Scripture, and allowing Him to bring light into the dark spaces in your life. Lament is a powerful way to express your pain to the Lord, and speaking unspoken grief to the Lord in the pattern of the lament Psalms can help you find release.

Forgive and let go Forgiveness does not excuse harm; it helps you break the cycle of resentment and harm as you release the grip of the past on who you are and will be.

Set new patterns Make intentional choices empowered by God’s Spirit and grace to create new family traditions, communicate in a different style, and so on.

Seek counseling A trained Christian counselor can help you identify and unpack the deep wounds and trauma, break harmful patterns of thinking and behavior, and begin building healthier responses to everyday life.

Through faith-based counseling alongside trauma-informed therapies such as internal family systems or cognitive behavioral therapy, your counselor can help you process these deep wounds in a safe environment.

Healing the wounds of the past can start with you today. Reach out to our office or contact our reception team to connect with a counselor who can walk with you on your journey toward healing and wholeness.

References

  • Yehuda, R., & Lehrner, A. (2018). Intergenerational transmission of trauma effects: Putative role of epigenetic mechanisms. World Psychiatry, 17(3), 243–257. https://doi.org/10.1002/wps.20568
  • Isobel, S., Goodyear, M., Furness, T., & Foster, K. (2019). Preventing intergenerational trauma transmission: A critical interpretive synthesis. Journal of Clinical Nursing, 28(7–8), 1100–1113. https://doi.org/10.1111/jocn.14735
  • Narayan, A. J., Lieberman, A. F., & Masten, A. S. (2021). Intergenerational transmission and prevention of adverse childhood experiences (ACEs). Clinical Psychology Review, 85, 101997.

item.title: Considering Therapy? Discover Topics Covered in Therapy for Women
item.description:
Women are more likely to seek help for their mental health, according to the National Center for Health Statistics. This is good news. But you don’t have to wait until you feel like you can no longer bear a situation. Counseling centers use therapy for women for a multitude of topics.

Common Topics Covered in Therapy for Women

Women assume roles inside and outside the home. They serve as caregivers to families, friends, and the church. Many mothers and grandmothers also volunteer for organizations, including those in which their children or grandchildren are involved.

They pour out so much of themselves into others that they may not notice that they themselves are depleted. Hormonal shifts, life events, and other problems can take a toll on their physical and mental health.

We talk with women about a variety of topics at our center. The following are the common topics covered in therapy for women.

Trauma-Specific

Whether from abuse, neglect, abandonment, violence, or natural disasters, we see women trying to move past trauma. Trauma brings about nightmares, anxiety, depression, negative thoughts, fears, and a host of other issues. Trauma-specific issues often affect physical health.

Your counselor will get to know you and discuss a treatment plan for your specific situation while addressing you as a whole person. Christian counseling is more than just the mind. We want to help you thrive in your physical, mental, emotional, and spiritual health.

Body Image Issues

Body image issues can stem from societal pressures, childhood experiences, or sudden changes in body composition. However, not every thought is true. You should always challenge negative thoughts, a skill you can learn in counseling. Sometimes perception plays a huge role in how women view themselves. Body image issues can lead to body dysmorphia, eating disorders, and low self-esteem.

Relationships

Relationships with a significant other, parents, children, and extended family can cause distress if there is contention. Toxic relationships and friendships that leave you drained and feeling worse after being around them will erode your confidence. Some of these relationships feel painful. Counseling can show you how to be assertive and place distance if needed by teaching you how to set (and enforce) boundaries.

Life Events

One of the most common topics we cover in therapy for women is the transition into roles during major life events. All major life changes come with some stress, even the good ones. Stress and doubt may prevail as a woman tries to adjust or adapt to her new normal. Graduations, marriages, deaths, births, moves, and career changes can leave a woman feeling out of control and on edge.

Anxiety and Depression

Anxiety and depression are common mental health disorders we treat at our center. Chronic stress, hormonal changes, life changes, chemical imbalances, and other factors contribute to mental health conditions.

Arming a woman with strategies and techniques to overcome anxiety and depression and move forward is our goal. We want every woman to leave a session feeling empowered, not only by herself, but with God’s help.

Contact Us to Learn More about Therapeutic Approaches in Christian Counseling

Our office would love to work with you. Our representatives can connect you with a Christian counselor specializing in therapy for women. Therapeutic approaches can include talk therapy, group therapy, Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), and more. Contact us today for an assessment.

item.title: Why Am I So Angry All the Time? Practical Tips to Overcome Anger
item.description:
The Heart Angle

It is important to discuss anger from a heartfelt perspective, although anger is not known for being a heartfelt emotion. When a person asks why they are so angry all the time, the root cause may not be known, so the question will only be partially answered.

The root cause for a great deal of the anger that is experienced derives from issues or matters of the heart. There is a saying that says there is a thin line between love and hate. Indeed, it is so thin that at times their distance from one another is small.

As a therapist, I have found that when anger is unpacked, it often stems from heartbreak caused by disappointment, loss, grief, lack of progress, feelings of failure, rejection, abandonment, and even a lack of felt love. Anger is often telling you what you are avoiding.

Emotions are the byproduct of the deeper symptoms. What is going on in your heart that is portraying itself as anger? To answer this question, we must go underneath. Your anger is trying to tell you something. The question is: what? This is often what is occurring.

  • There is hurt without clarity.
  • Undealt-with rejection.
  • Unhealed abandonment.
  • You may be feeling powerless.
  • You may be feeling ignored.
  • You may have tolerated something for too long.
  • You may be feeling stuck.
  • You may even be angry because there is a truth somewhere in your life that you have been unwilling or unable to confront.

Take the time to consider each thought. Allow it to sit with you.

Anger and Our Relationship with the Truth

I believe a great deal of anger can be connected to our relationship with truth. Sometimes we are angry because we cannot tell the truth. Sometimes we are angry because we do not want to face the truth. Sometimes we are angry because we are not living according to what we know is true.

Then there are times when we are angry because someone else told us the truth and we were not ready to hear it. The truth can be uncomfortable. Truth can seem threatening. Truth can even seem insulting without the intention of being so.

Maybe you continue saying yes to people when you really want to push back. Yet the deeper problem may not be that people keep asking. The deeper problem may be that you have not been honest about what you can handle. You have trouble admitting your limitations, and you would rather die than have anyone perceive a weakness.

Perhaps you are angry about your lack of professional progression. You are feeling overlooked by your superiors and undervalued. You resent your coworkers for getting what you deserve. You used to love your company and once saw a future there. But now you dread work mornings. Deep down, you know it is time to make a change, but fear has prevented you from making a change.

Truth will also require you to acknowledge when you have participated in your own frustration. There are times when we remain in situations long after we know something must change. Nevertheless, we become angry with people for crossing boundaries we have never verbalized or enforced.

We may even become irritated when others do not recognize needs that we have never expressed. Standing toe to toe with truth means asking yourself what part of the situation belongs to you. That moment may be uncomfortable, but it can help show us where we still have the power to move differently.

Your anger is real. But so is the hurtful and hard-to-face truth underneath it. Jesus said that the truth would make us free. Freedom has never begun with pretending. Freedom requires us to become willing to see what is there. Sometimes anger increases because we are fighting reality that we feel helpless to change.

Think About It, You May Not Be Angry About Today

A major reason why anger can feel disproportionate is that the current situation is carrying the weight of several previous situations. Someone does something tiny, and in return you respond enormously. Ever wonder when you became so upset? The other person may wonder the same thing.

The answer could be that you were not only responding to what happened today, because that is all you can see in the moment. However, you neglected to really comprehend that you were responding to every time you felt overlooked. Not to mention every time you were disappointed, or for each time a promise was broken, or for each conversation that went unresolved.

Think about it, you may not be angry about today, but for every moment you have decided not to say anything. Your anger had been accumulating when experiences that you had in your life were not properly processed. This is why it is not unusual to encounter some people going from zero to one hundred over something that appears insignificant.

The current situation may simply be the final place where everything else came to a head. In those intense moments, ask yourself, “What else am I responding to right now?” The answer could separate today’s frustration from yesterday’s wound.

Practical Tips to Overcome Anger

The goal of overcoming anger is not to become a person who never gets angry. This is unrealistic and not maintainable. The key to overcoming anger is learning how to recognize what your anger is revealing before it begins attempting to take center stage. Your anger becomes more manageable when you have practical steps that can help you move from reacting to your anger toward understanding it and responding differently.

Identify what is happening beneath the anger Instead of “I am upset,” finish the sentence: “I am angry because I felt…” Permit yourself to go above and beyond what may have been your obvious answer. Were you feeling ashamed? Did you feel disregarded? Did you feel powerless? Remember, naming what is at the root of your anger will aid you in understanding what really needs your attention,

Start separating what you can change from what you cannot control Ask: “What am I avoiding?” You may already know what needs to be changed. The hard part may be accepting what that truth may require from us.

Do not shut down speaking what you feel sooner Do not make silence carry something until anger has to announce it. You cannot control another person’s choices. You can control what you participate in. You can decide what you will tolerate. You can also determine what access someone will continue to have to you.

Examine your expectations Determine what was conveyed. Do not make silence carry something until anger has to announce it. Learn to communicate frustration while it is still frustration. Not everything requires confrontation, but important matters should not continually be buried.

Decide what you should be grieving instead of correcting Some things cannot be fixed. They must be mourned. Some things cannot be fixed. They must be mourned. You may be trying to get an apology you will never receive or attempting to change something that has already happened. Grief may be necessary where correction is no longer possible.

Choose what your anger will yield Let it lead to a boundary, conversation, decision, healing work, or change rather than damage. Anger has energy attached to it. Decide where that energy will go. Your anger can destroy something or reveal what needs to be different. The responsibility is deciding what happens next.

item.title: True Transformation: Rewiring the Brain with Healthy Thoughts
item.description:
Have you ever thought, “I want transformation but don’t know how to achieve it”? Or “Why am I not experiencing lasting change?” Have you tried hard to make some changes in your life, but you still feel little to no progress? Or maybe you experienced some good changes, but they did not last long? What is the key to authentic and lasting transformation? The answer is in our thoughts.

The Garden Image

Let me explain with an image. Imagine your mental health is a large garden. The goal is to keep the garden flourishing with good plant life, which will represent mental health wellness. Now imagine the problem you are facing is a standard garden weed. The weed is toxic to your garden and must be removed. The weed can be anxiety, anger outbursts, depression, addiction, trauma, relationship discord, etc.

Removing the weed will keep away significant damage to your mental health. Some people will attempt to fix the problem by removing the stems and leaves and anything else they can see above the soil. They walk away thinking, “The weed is gone, so the problem is solved.” But they return in a few months to find that the same garden weed returned with more leaves and stems. How could it possibly have grown back?

As you can guess, the roots of the weed remained in the soil, which only made the problem appear to be gone. The person failed to pull the garden weed out by the roots. As long as the roots remain, the problem remains, which means no real lasting change can take place.

Now let me give some explanation of what the different parts of the weed represent. The stems and leaves of the garden weed represent behaviors and feelings. The roots of the garden weed represent our thoughts.

Understandably, we focus on the behaviors quite a bit to fix the problem because it is what we are seeing. Behaviors are everything from substance use and running away to playing and laughing. We can try to change our behaviors and feelings all day long but still have no real lasting change. Psychology teaches us that our thoughts affect our emotions and then our emotions affect our behaviors, and then our behaviors create our experiences.

So, for authentic and lasting change to take place, we need to examine the thoughts because they are the root, the epicenter, of everything that is happening. We must examine the deepest part of ourselves because this holds the greatest power to affect our entire psyche. This means that (in this image) the root of the weed needs to be fully removed in order for there to be change.

But it does not stop there. Not only does the root of the weed need to be removed, but it also needs to be replaced with a far healthier plant (a healthier thought). When we have healthy thoughts, incredible, lasting transformation starts to take place.

Rewiring the Brain

So now that we understand that the root of the garden weed is toxic thoughts (untruthful, unhelpful, distorted thinking), what do we do about it? The answer is in rewiring the brain.

God created our brains in a way to have the ability to remap and rewire themselves. Romans 12:2 states, “Do not conform to the pattern of this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind.” In today’s world, we know this concept formally as neuroplasticity and cognitive restructuring.

Neuroplasticity is the remarkable ability of the nervous system to change, adapt, and reorganize its physical structure and functional connections throughout your life. It is the biological mechanism that allows the brain to learn new skills, recover from injuries, and adapt to changing environments.

This means that the transformation we seek doesn’t begin with changing circumstances or relationships. Transformation starts in our minds. We must shift the way we think in order to get the transformation we want. So, let’s begin by understanding some basic neuroscience.

Every time you have a thought, a neural pathway is created or reused in your brain. The more you have a particular thought, the stronger that neural pathway becomes and eventually becomes an automatic thought. Automatic thoughts are pathways in our mind that we have used so many times that they are instantly the way we think about a certain situation, person, or stimulus.

The first thing to do is to record these thoughts, formally known as a Thought Record. In the world of cognitive behavioral therapy, we call this cognitive restructuring. We select one thought at a time and put it on trial to challenge its validity. We ask, “Is this true? Is this hurting me or helping me? Is this thought based on objective facts?” When we find that a thought is untruthful, distorted, and only hurting us, we can then identify that as a toxic thought.

Once we have identified a toxic thought, we then select a replacement thought that is truthful, healthy, and helpful. God, being the divine architect of our brains, knows that the way to fix toxic thinking is by deliberately focusing our thoughts on what is healthy and helpful. Philippians 4:13 instructs us to focus our thoughts on what is true, noble, right, pure, lovely, admirable, excellent, and praiseworthy.

And again, science is just now catching up to this. Neuroscience proves Philippians 4:13 by showing us how new neural pathways form when we have a thought. Studies and research conclude that healthy, helpful thoughts bring life and wellness to our bodies.

The antidote to toxic thinking is to intentionally focus on and rehash thoughts that are true, noble, right, pure, lovely, admirable, excellent, and praiseworthy. This is the game changer. So, the only way to make that toxic thought stop is to replace it with a new thought.

Now the next part takes discipline and practice. We live in a culture of fast-paced results, but our brain does not operate in the same way. Our brain needs significant repetition to wire in an automatic thought. The studies and research on neuroplasticity have found that the new thought needs to be rehearsed enough to get wired into the brain.

In one study, participants were directed to rehearse their new healthy thought by taking five minutes every day to repeat the healthy thought out loud or write it down over and over again. The results showed that many participants had successfully rewired their brain with the new healthy thought by day sixty-three. The toxic thought naturally eased in intensity, and for many, the toxic thought ceased.

The new wiring of healthy thought results in more positive emotions (peace, optimism, contentment) and then creates more desired behaviors (restful sleep, connecting with others, responding calmly to stress). This is what we want in our mental health garden. Pulling out weeds and then planting healthy plants is the key to lasting change.

Remember, your life will not change until your mind changes. You are only limited by how you see yourself and how you choose to think. Your mind and thoughts are the game changer to true and lasting transformation.

How To Rewire Your Mind

Write down all your thoughts (a Thought Record)

Put your thoughts on trial Determine whether it is healthy, helpful, and truthful, or untruthful, hurtful, and toxic.

To help determine if the thought is healthy or toxic, ask the following: Is this based on facts? What are the objective facts here? Did I confirm that my interpretation is based on reality? Did the person actually say that to me? Is there another way I could look at this? Did that actually happen? Does this thought make me feel worse, or does it make things feel more manageable?

Select a new healthy thought

Working on this with a therapist or good friend is always helpful because they can offer a new way of thinking about this thought that you likely have not considered before.

Meditate on this new thought through active repetition every day Reserve five minutes every day to rehearse the new healthy thought by saying it out loud or writing it. Continue this routine until the new thought becomes an automatic thought. Anticipate about two months to notice real change and a transformation that lasts a lifetime.

Repeat this process with every toxic thought This is a lifelong skill to commit to.

Example

The automatic thought: “I can’t do anything right.”

Challenge the thought with questions: What exactly do I feel I have not done right? Is it really true that everything I have done is wrong? Is this thought hurting me or is it helping me?

Consider the answers: This thought makes me feel bad, which means it is hurting me. No, it is not true that everything I have done is wrong. I have indeed done a few things wrong because my coworker verbally told me that I did not complete certain tasks needed before closing the shop. But there are a lot of things I have done correctly at work. I know this because my supervisor thanked me for the good work.

Select a new healthy thought: “Sometimes I make mistakes. I am human, I am not perfect, and mistakes are part of life. There are a lot of things I do correctly. I can choose to learn from my mistakes.”

item.title: Anger Management Strategies to Help You Control Your Anger
item.description:
Anger is a powerful emotion that can derail your life if you allow it. Not only can unbridled anger cloud your judgment, but it can also rob you of your sense of peace while damaging relationships, sometimes irreparably. As troublesome as it is, we should remember that anger isn’t necessarily sinful or against God’s will for our lives. Scripture reminds us, “Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger.” (Ephesians 4:26, ESV)

While anger isn’t necessarily sinful, the challenge that we all face is that anger can be difficult to manage. It’s way too easy for justifiable or righteous anger to quickly morph into the sort of anger that dishonors the Lord and others. What starts well and good can become damaging to your relational, emotional, and mental well-being. Having good anger management strategies can help you maintain a healthy balance.

Unpacking the Impact of Anger

When you feel anger rising inside of you, usually it’s because it’s been triggered by something. You may have been snubbed at work by a colleague, or your loved one left you feeling unheard. Perhaps someone took advantage of you, or you witnessed something manifestly unjust. Whatever it is, one of the emotional responses to such situations is anger, and that anger is often appropriate.

Anger can be overwhelming, and indulging it may seem so rewarding in the moment. Letting choice words fly at someone who cut you off in traffic can give you a sense of accomplishment or victory. I sure told them, we might say to ourselves. It is way too easy to go over the line and say too much, say something you regret, or act recklessly without regard to how those words or actions feel to other people.

It may be helpful to picture anger like a wild bronco that may have placid moments, but that can change in an instant. It’s not wise to turn your back or let your guard down around them. Uncontrolled anger can wreak havoc in your life by stirring up conflict, leading you to utter hurtful words you otherwise wouldn’t, or taking you down the path to actions you later regret.

There is a Proverb that says, “An angry person stirs up conflict, and a hot-tempered person commits many sins.” (Proverbs 29:22, NIV) If anger begins controlling you, it becomes a chronic problem. Such anger has spiritual consequences, such as derailing your walk with the Lord (James 1:19-22). Chronic anger can also increase your stress levels and negatively impact your physical health by increasing your blood pressure and the risk of heart disease.

Besides these effects of uncontrolled anger, there can be a relational cost to anger, too. Anger can create deep wounds between loved ones, and those wounds can be slow to heal. Anger can also build walls between people, especially when that anger makes them feel unsafe around you. Anger, then, can be quite devastating.

The Blessings of Better Anger Management

The above probably gives anger a bad rap by pointing out all of the negative impacts of anger. Remember, anger isn’t sinful in itself. There is something to be said for dealing with anger in a healthy and constructive way. Anger can be a tool used for growth and renewal, and it’s not just destructive.

An example of this is when you feel unheard by a loved one. The feelings of anger can be handled well or poorly. The unhealthy route would include giving them the silent treatment in response or shouting at them to make yourself heard. The healthy option would include listening to that anger and discerning what lies at the root of it, and then pursuing dialogue with your loved one.

It is possible to express anger in healthy ways that build stronger relationships. Anger can function like a check engine light to let you know what’s happening inside you. Responding appropriately to those cues helps you communicate your needs effectively with others. This can mean fostering deeper trust and intimacy when you give gentle responses to tense situations.

Being in control of your anger and managing it well can also mean better health as you lower your stress levels, open yourself up more to the Lord’s peace, and yield more and more to the Spirit’s guidance. You’re better able to live well with yourself and with others when you can manage your emotions effectively.

Why Some Anger Management Strategies Fail

There are many benefits to managing your anger well. However, there are pitfalls along that path, and being aware of them can help you to be fruitful as you try to keep your anger in check.

Anger management strategies can fail or fall short when they are only skin deep. There is a strategy where you count slowly down from ten, and it’s a way to help you slow down before you respond rashly. This strategy does work in the moment, but it’s important to address the underlying heart issues. Anger can resurface and become harder to control.

Sticking with anger management strategies can also be difficult if you’re relying solely on willpower. For sustained and lasting change, we need the Lord’s help as well as accountability from others. The encouragement and support we get from other people can help us stay on the path, and the work of the Spirit in us can bring about true transformation in our hearts.

In other circumstances, anger management strategies don’t stick because we ignore the root causes of anger. Anger may be a momentary response, but many other things, such as learned patterns of behavior, often inform it. Other underlying causes of anger could be stress, unforgiveness, or unresolved trauma, which can fuel your anger and unhealthy responses to situations.

Awareness of these potential pitfalls can help you make good use of anger management strategies that help you keep anger in check. At the same time, you can address the deeper issues that could be informing your anger.

Effective Anger Management Strategies to Help You Control Anger

There are many strategies that you can use to help you manage your anger. It’s important to remember that anger management isn’t about suppressing your anger or pretending it doesn’t exist. Those are different ways of handling anger poorly. Rather, the goal is to develop a healthy relationship with your anger, to be able to understand your own anger, and channel it constructively instead of letting it take the reins.

Some effective anger management strategies include the following:

Pause, and pray: Allow yourself to count down from ten, or to leave the room briefly when you can, to allow yourself space to calm down. Stepping out of the situation can make a difference. When you feel anger rising, pause, breathe, and pray. Ask the Lord to help you stay calm and respond wisely, instead of being guided by your emotions.

Identify your triggers: Your anger works in ways that are unique to you. Reflect on the situations that tend to make your anger flare up. Recognize your own patterns of anger, like when you’re tired, hungry, stressed, or feeling vulnerable. Knowing these patterns helps you to anticipate your anger and manage it before it flares up or escalates.

Reframe your thoughts: Often, anger can be magnified because of our thinking patterns. If someone makes a hurtful joke or comment, it might not necessarily be intentional. Assuming it is can cause anger to flare up. It’s better to presume otherwise until you have further information. Meditating on Scripture about patience and self-control can also help to reshape your responses to triggering situations.

Use healthy outlets: Anger ought to be expressed, and there are healthy ways to do this. Using art or other forms of creative expression like writing, exercise and other physical activity, or talking things out with a trusted confidante can help you to release the tension of anger without damaging yourself or other people.

Practice forgiveness: Grudges and resentment can harbor and nurture anger. Instead, choose to forgive, releasing yourself from the burden of resentment or the need to get even.

Develop communication and problem-solving skills: There are times when you feel angry because you feel helpless or can’t express your concerns clearly. When you can plan and act to overcome challenges, and when you can work through issues amicably, it can prevent frustrations from taking over.

Seek help: Anger management therapy can help you dig deep to understand the underlying causes of your anger. You can also learn how to reframe your thoughts and implement strategies to help keep your anger under control. Help isn’t far from you; reach out to our office to connect with an anger management counselor today.

item.title: Breaking Out of the Sleep Anxiety Spiral
item.description:
Some people get to a certain age, and they realize that they have been exhausted for months or even years. Sleep loss affects an array of people, from teens in the middle of exams, new parents adjusting to the demands of an infant, or elderly people dealing with rapid changes in their lives. Some people are simply tired because events like these are demanding, but many people are tired because they have sleep anxiety.

Sleep anxiety is not the same as insomnia; it is the things that cause insomnia. It is the fear you start to feel as bedtime nears, as you worry that you will not fall asleep. It is the dread you feel when you wake up in the middle of the night and see that it is only midnight. You spend hours in bed, willing yourself to sleep, but failing. You can’t help but think about your day tomorrow and the consequences of losing sleep.

Sleep anxiety is debilitating, but it can be fixed without medication or substances. Studies have shown that medication does not help with sleep anxiety in the long-term. When you begin to understand what is going on in your head and in your body, you will begin to unpack some of the anxiety surrounding your sleep problems, breaking the sleep anxiety spiral. Your overthinking might be the thing driving your sleep anxiety, but your mind is also the solution.

The Sleep Anxiety Spiral

The most frustrating thing about sleep anxiety is that it is self-perpetuating. You stress about not being able to fall asleep or stay asleep, and it is that stress that causes sleeplessness. It is like being so afraid of failing your driving test that you cannot concentrate and end up failing the test. It is a form of self-fulfilling prophecy.

Sleep anxiety doesn’t only cause you stress in the evenings, but it also affects your daytime routine. Many people believe that they can only function properly on eight solid hours of sleep per day. This is a common idea that intensifies sleep anxiety. It looks like this: you believe that you need eight hours of quality sleep per day, and so you become anxious that you won’t get that. Then it is your anxiety over not getting enough sleep that becomes the very thing preventing you from getting enough sleep.

There are things you can do and things you must keep from doing to break the sleep anxiety spiral. Overall, you must change your approach to sleep, change the way you think about sleep, and make some changes to your routine. By interrupting your thoughts and behavior this way, you are creating a new pattern for yourself, and it can adapt to your new lifestyle.

Things You Must Do to Interrupt Sleep Anxiety

There are several practical things that you can start doing to interrupt the sleep anxiety spiral. It is a good idea to speak with a doctor or specialist before starting this new regimen, or with anyone who can keep you accountable and provide support. These ideas range from simple tips to deeper and broader attitude changes.

Firstly, create a healthy bedtime routine and stick to it. Your body has a function called the circadian rhythm. This is a set of automatic responses that your central nervous system performs throughout the day to help you. When your brain registers that it is nearing bedtime, it will release a hormone called melatonin into your nervous system. This hormone brings down your cortisol levels, puts your bladder and bowels on pause for the night, and generally prepares your body to be inactive for the next eight to ten hours.

You can help your circadian rhythm in practical ways by following a 3-2-1 principle. Have your final meal of the night three hours before bedtime, have your final drink two hours before bedtime, and reduce screen time for the last hour before bed. This will prime your body for sleep even if your mind is overactive.

With sleep anxiety, you struggle to fall asleep, and you struggle to stay asleep. The first thing most people do when they wake up is to look at the clock and calculate how many hours of sleep they have left. Try taking away your ability to time-check. Remove clocks from your bedroom and place your phone far away from your bedside. This interrupts the compulsive time-checking and the anxiety that comes with it.

In a larger sense, you must change the way you think about sleeping. For example, you might believe that you can only function during the day if you have had more than six hours of sleep the night before.

The truth is that you can be perfectly functional on minimal sleep, even over a long period of time. New parents experience years of sleeplessness and still manage to get by successfully. Sometimes it is your internal beliefs about sleep that contribute the most to sleep anxiety.

Lean into the idea that you are going to be tired tomorrow, and that it’s okay. Accept whatever amount of sleep you get, whether it’s only a few solid hours. Think of nighttime as rest time rather than sleep time.

The fact that you are lying down in a relaxed, safe environment and not looking at screens is enough for your body; sleep would be a bonus. When you change the way you think about sleep, sleep anxiety begins to lose its footing and influence over your mind.

Things to Avoid While Dealing with Sleep Anxiety

It’s natural to feel helpless and overwhelmed with sleep anxiety, and many people resort to using medication and substances like alcohol to cope. These things might help get you some sleep occasionally, but there is a real danger of becoming dependent on them over time. If you have been using medication or substances to help with sleep anxiety, aim to stop using them entirely.

Avoiding screen time before bed and keeping clocks out of sight is good, but it’s also a good idea to get up if you wake up at a certain time. When you lie in bed chasing sleep, you tend to begin overthinking and stressing.

You could try using mindfulness techniques or tools like brain shuffling to get back to sleep, but it’s a better idea to get up and go to a quiet spot in the house for some reading or crafting. Try to avoid screens still, and it’s best not to eat or drink anything. Instead, doing a relaxed activity in a dimly lit room will help keep the anxiety at bay. Eventually, you will become sleepy again, at which point you can simply return to bed to sleep.

Many sleep-tracking apps try to address insomnia, but these have the opposite effect on sleep anxiety. When you have a visualization for how much sleep you’re not getting, that intensifies the anxiety you feel. The goal is to be rested, not to get the perfect amount of sleep each night. Avoid tracking your sleep or trying to meet sleep goals. Instead, aim to have a restful evening. If you fall asleep for a few hours, that’s great. If you don’t, it’s not the end of the world.

Sleep anxiety is difficult, but it’s a cycle you can break. It might not happen overnight, but if you can get to a place where you feel more rested and less anxious, you will have made incredible progress. Give yourself a break because you deserve it.

Some things are easier to face and overcome with someone on your side. Consider meeting with a counselor if your sleep anxiety has become overwhelming. If you don’t have a counselor, we hope that you can find someone suitable in our online catalog or by enlisting the help of our reception team.

item.title: When to Seek PTSD Help So You Can Feel Better
item.description:
Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) is a mental condition affecting roughly 13 million people in the United States annually. The trauma disorder interferes with daily activities if left untreated, as well as disrupts relationships and responsibilities.

Knowing when to seek help can enable you to work with a counselor to build a customized plan for managing symptoms of PTSD.

Signs to Seek PTSD Help

The symptoms of PTSD can cause mental distress and physical issues. Unfortunately, many people may be unaware that the anxiety they feel is Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder. People seek PTSD help after the following:

  • Involved in a violent event, such as war
  • Witnessing a traumatic event
  • Being abandoned, neglected, or abused
  • Being under great pressure for a period of time, such as caregiving for a terminal loved one

Anyone can develop PTSD, not just war veterans, although that is the demographic most associated with PTSD. For example, a woman caring for her terminal mother may develop PTSD symptoms due to chronic stress and worry. A teenage boy may show symptoms if he was neglected or abused during early childhood.

Christian counseling is effective for managing PTSD symptoms. Your counselor will combine evidence-based techniques with faith-based principles to address you as a whole person: physically, mentally, and spiritually.

The following are signs that you may need PTSD help.

Persistent Reactions

If you experience persistent reactions to noise or other triggers, you could be showing a sign of PTSD. People who have experienced trauma often physically react to triggers. For example, a war veteran may duck when they hear a loud bang. A woman may suffer a panic attack during a storm because she lived through a natural disaster, such as a tornado.

Startling, ducking, and high anxiety due to a trigger that occurs for more than four weeks indicate that a mental health professional should see you. Counseling is not lifelong. You learn the skills you need to manage and overcome PTSD symptoms spread out over several sessions.

Interference with Daily Life

Memories and traumatic behavior (like the startle response or panic attacks) can interfere with your daily activities. You may find yourself withdrawing from others or preferring to work from home. You may feel embarrassment, guilt, or shame in your reactions.

Yet, isolation is never the answer. Learning to overcome panic attacks, anxiety, depression, and intrusive memories can bolster your self-esteem and confidence. You are a work in progress, and God never intended for you to walk through this alone. Counseling and support can help you get back to what is important to you.

Intrusive Thoughts

Intrusive thoughts and memories are strong, vivid images and urges. If you suffer from PTSD, you may have experienced these. Intrusive thoughts can be scary and seem to come out of nowhere. They can make you want to give in and do things you wouldn’t normally do. Sometimes, these thoughts can feel true. False beliefs arise from intrusive thoughts.

Intrusive memories can appear as realistic flashbacks. Some people have experienced such vivid flashbacks that the line between reality and memory blurs. It can take several minutes to return to reality, though the physical effects (rapid heart rate, shallow breathing, high blood pressure) can persist for hours.

Emotional Symptoms

Intense emotions can plague someone dealing with PTSD. Shame, guilt, sadness, and anger can stem from the event or chronic situation that has led to the trauma disorder. You may feel empty and numb, detached from others around you, and unable to connect with friends and family.

Thought distortions about yourself or others can cause riffs where none exist. Paranoia can also contribute to feelings of loneliness. The emotional upheaval can lead to other anxiety and depressive disorders if left untreated.

Physical Symptoms

The mind is a powerful thing. Anxiety and depression can fuel changes in brain chemistry and the nervous system. Physical symptoms can develop, including:

  • Rapid or irregular heart rate
  • High blood pressure
  • Appetite changes
  • Rapid weight gain or loss
  • Poor sleep quality
  • Forgetfulness or brain fog
  • Unexplainable pain
  • Digestive issues
  • Headaches
  • Skin rashes or itchiness

Physical and emotional symptoms can combine to leave you feeling unworthy and isolated from the world. If you or someone you love is having thoughts of harming themselves or others, or struggles with suicidal thoughts, seek help immediately.

Counseling for PTSD

If you are seeking PTSD help, we can assist you in your search. Contact us today to speak to a representative who will connect you to a Christian counselor specializing in trauma disorders. PTSD help is only a call or click away.

item.title: The Emotional Toll of Resentment and the Impact of Godly Forgiveness
item.description:
Bitterness from old wounds left unattended can creep in like a shadow, unexpected and quiet. It brawls with forgiveness, which is the key to emotional freedom. This freedom feels like it’s impossible to grasp as we try to let go of the bitterness in ourselves. We carry this bitterness in strained marriages or fractured friendships, and we hold on to something that seems to erode the soul.

This inward discomfort of appearing strong but inwardly breaking results in a silent struggle. Christian counselors are familiar with this tension, and they can provide a faith-based approach to help focus on the pain rather than trying to bury it. This requires confronting what has caused the bitterness to achieve true and godly forgiveness.

Resentment can develop in layers, starting with a single sharp moment and building into repeated disappointments. If left unchecked, it will subtly alter the way we perceive daily interactions. This will lead us to be more sensitive to any offense and less responsive to encouragement. Eventually, a wall is built between our hearts and the hearts of others, as well as God’s, leading to a barrier that cannot be broken without intentional, spiritual practice.

The Roots of Bitterness

It just takes one spark of betrayal, unmet hope, or a slight to ignite resentment. The longer it is left alone, the deeper it grows, and it replays in the mind like a broken record. This isn’t just anger. It’s a deep sense of injustice. While society pushes us to move on, we find that the wound is deeper, and we have become guarded.

In relationships, the result of this resentment is distance. We begin to feel right and, at the same time, alone, as if we are wearing a mask and hiding the pain behind a façade of strength. Christian counselors can guide us through a process, peeling back the layers to reveal how bitterness distorts our views of others and ourselves. The struggle is often personal and tied to identity, so holding on feels powerful, yet it is chaining us to the past.

Bitterness can be like an infection in our souls. Unforgiven hurts will spill into unrelated areas of life and color our judgment and even our memories. We find that we will start filtering our past interactions through a lens of resentment and rewriting history in a way that causes our pain to become concrete.

It is vital to recognize this pattern, as spiritual healing can only begin with acknowledging the truth. If we choose to allow God to illuminate these hidden corners, we will see ourselves become transformed.

A heart at peace gives life to the body, but envy rots the bones. – Proverbs 14:30, NIV

Mental Health Consequences of Harboring Resentment

Bitterness is a heavy burden that can deplete both the mind and body. It will fuel anxiety, cloud our focus, and disrupt our sleep. The result is a stress response that stays on and wears us down. This isn’t just an emotional issue, as resentment can raise blood pressure and weaken the immune system.

Emotionally, it will breed distrust and make it difficult to connect with others. Joy will fade, and it will be replaced with cynicism. On the outside, we may seem fine, but on the inside, it looks as though we are unraveling from our very core. This contradictory sense of self is where bitterness thrives, unnoticed and destructive. Christian counselors can help us recognize the cycle and learn how to release grudges before they spiral out of control.

It is known that chronic resentment increases the risk of depression and even cognitive decline. This is not just psychological research, but it is also biblical wisdom. Forgiveness nurtures resilience and helps rewire the brain to reduce stress responses. Engaging in prayer time can help create a mental shift that improves spiritual health and enhances overall well-being. Consider the words of Paul in Ephesians:

Get rid of all bitterness, rage and anger, brawling and slander, along with every form of malice. Be kind and compassionate to one another, forgiving each other, just as in Christ God forgave you. – Ephesians 4:31-32, NIV

The Path to Forgiveness

Forgiveness starts with honesty and the ability to name the hurt without excusing it. It will shift us from being a victim to being in control of letting go. This isn’t an easy process; grudges feel like shields. One way to navigate the process without judgment is to learn how to express emotions in words through journaling. Over time, we will develop the strength to face the pain.

The next step is to choose empathy. This requires that we acknowledge our own flaws. It doesn’t make the wrong right, but it does soften our hearts, allowing forgiveness to come in a godly way. Praying for peace is another small step that will pave the way to forgiveness.

This process doesn’t fix everything overnight, but it is a daily choice that breaks the grip of resentment. The path may be uneven, but with each step, the load is lightened, and we find peace over revenge.

Another way to lighten the burden of resentment is to seek support. This can be done by sharing with a trusted friend or a Christian counselor who can help create space for healing. This doesn’t mean that we would relive the hurt, but instead we would learn to reframe it by looking at it through a lens of grace. This becomes a step toward forgiveness that is grounded in community and faith.

The Bible encourages us, “Bear with each other and forgive one another if any of you has a grievance against someone. Forgive as the Lord forgave you.” (Colossians 3:13, NIV)

Embracing Biblical Forgiveness

Biblical forgiveness is a reflection of God’s mercy, and it’s not optional. It is a call for us to mirror the grace that Christ showed us. Starting with prayer, we can ask for strength to release grudges. This will require us to be honest in our relationships and not bottle up the pain, so that we can build trust rather than walls.

Using this approach will transform our outlook. It will help us trade bitterness for compassion and align our lives with faith. Eventually, forgiveness will become a habit, freeing us from past hurts and opening space for joy. By embracing these changes, we can see ourselves and others differently and become grounded in the truth of God’s word.

Embracing biblical forgiveness means setting boundaries with wisdom. We don’t ignore the harm, but instead, we choose to release its hold through God’s strength. By doing this, we can protect our hearts and foster healing. Christian counselors can guide us in this process and help us to align forgiveness with our faith.

In Matthew, Jesus gives clear guidelines about forgiveness: “‘For if you forgive other people when they sin against you, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. But if you do not forgive others their sins, your Father will not forgive your sins.’” (Matthew 6:14-15, NIV)

Finding Freedom from Resentment

Bitterness will bind us, but godly forgiveness will set us free and heal our minds and spirits. Isolation will be replaced with connection. When we reflect on grudges that we carry, we can determine if they are worth the cost.

Scripture will always lead us to a better way, one immersed in grace and release. We must remember that forgiveness isn’t weakness but rather strength in Christ. Christian counselors can help us learn to lean on God and step into his peace.

For help with resentment and forgiveness, make an appointment with a Christian counselor. Browse the directory to find someone you can talk to.

item.title: Understanding the Types of BPD and Their Connection to Substance Abuse
item.description:
Borderline personality disorder (BPD) affects how individuals experience themselves and relate to the world around them. Seeking relief from the emotional intensity that comes with BPD, individuals sometimes turn to substance abuse as a common coping mechanism. To understand why some people find themselves caught in patterns that they want to escape, we first have to understand the types of BPD and how they intersect with addiction.

There is a relationship between these two struggles that goes beyond a simple cause-and-effect. It reflects deeper questions about identity, managing pain, and a human need for stability. The way BPD manifests can determine not only how someone experiences their internal world, but which substances they turn to, and why. These distinctions are essential to break free from the cycle of emotional dysregulation and addiction.

Four Patterns Common Across the Multiple Types of BPD

Because each person is unique, borderline personality disorder doesn’t present the same way in everyone. Four primary patterns help explain the different ways that BPD manifests. These types of BPD are not meant to box people into categories concretely, but rather, they help us understand the ways emotional dysregulation shows up in real life. By recognizing which patterns resonate most with an individual, Christian counselors can guide treatment and offer hope that recovery is possible.

The discouraged type: This form of BPD often appears in people who seem dependent and seek constant reassurance while struggling with feelings of worthlessness. These individuals may appear passive or submissive in relationships and avoid confrontation, even when it would be healthy.

The impulsive type: Those who manifest this type of BPD often engage in risk-taking behaviors and emotional outbursts without concern for consequences. People who struggle with this form of BPD typically act on every feeling without pausing to consider the outcome, and they chase experiences that provide immediate gratification or distraction from inner emptiness.

The petulant type: This form of BPD involves stubborn negativity and feeling misunderstood, which results in pushing others away by simultaneously fearing abandonment. Individuals struggling with this pattern often feel like victims of their circumstances and may express bitterness or resentment toward those trying to help.

The self-destructive type: This pattern of BPD manifests in harmful behaviors directed inward, which include substance abuse, self-harm, or extreme risk-taking to manage unbearable emotional pain. Individuals of this type are the most visibly concerning. They seem intent on destroying themselves, even though self-harm isn’t about wanting to die. It’s about making internal pain visible.

Each of these patterns reflects a different strategy for managing the emotional dysregulation that is at the heart of BPD. Many individuals display characteristics from multiple types, and patterns can shift over time, so these categories are not considered rigid.

The consistency across these patterns is the intense fear of abandonment, unstable self-image, and difficulty regulating emotions that define the disorder. Adding substance abuse to this already intense struggle starts as an attempt to navigate the emotional turbulence that feels impossible to manage any other way.

Why Substance Abuse Co-Occurs with BPD

The connection between BPD and addiction is not coincidental. Most individuals diagnosed with BPD also struggle with substance use disorders. Because BPD creates an emotionally intense environment, substances often offer temporary relief from these struggles.

An individual experiencing rapid mood swings, chronic feelings of emptiness, and a fear of abandonment turns to alcohol or other substances to quiet the internal chaos. Substances only provide a brief escape from emotions that feel overwhelming and unmanageable.

Self-medication is not the only challenge with substance abuse and BPD. The brain chemistry is changed due to substance use, which can worsen BPD symptoms and create a cycle where each issue amplifies the other. Impulsivity is a core feature of BPD, and it can become more pronounced under the influence of substances, and emotional regulation becomes nearly impossible.

Christian counselors recognize that both conditions require integrated treatment. They emphasize that addressing one only leaves the underlying vulnerabilities untouched. The path to healing requires understanding how these struggles reinforce each other and learning how to cultivate healthier ways to cope with emotional pain. One good place to start is with encouraging Scriptures:

Cast your burden upon the Lord and He will sustain you; He will never allow the righteous to be shaken. – Psalm 55:22, NASB

How Different Types of BPD Influence Substance Use Patterns

A specific pattern of BPD often shapes the relationship an individual has with substances. Impulsive-type individuals engage in binge drinking or experiment with multiple substances, trying to find a thrill and temporary relief from boredom or inner emptiness.

Individuals who struggle with the self-destructive type of BPD may use substances deliberately to harm themselves or engage in dangerous combinations of risky behaviors. They are less concerned with pleasure and more focused on punishing themselves or numbing severe emotional pain.

Individuals who struggle with the discouraged type often use substances to cope with feelings of hopelessness and inadequacy. Using substances becomes an internal coping mechanism to numb the discouraging feelings.

The individual who suffers from the petulant type of BPD faces a more complex dynamic when it comes to substance use. They may engage in substance use in response to a perceived rejection or conflict. The result is a pattern where relationship struggles trigger substance use, which creates more relationship problems.

Christian counselors understand these patterns and can develop treatment approaches that address the specific needs of each individual who struggles with substance use and BPD. The goal is to build healthier ways to manage emotional experiences that made substances feel necessary in the first place.

Still, we are all reminded of Jesus’ words:

“Come to Me, all who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.” – Matthew 11:28, NASB

The Path Toward Integrated Healing

Co-occurring BPD and substance abuse recovery requires addressing both conditions simultaneously. If BPD remains untreated, traditional addiction treatment fails because the emotional dysregulation continues to drive the compulsion toward substances.

On the other hand, if BPD is treated without addressing active addiction, the treatment is ineffective because substances interfere with the ability to develop healthy coping strategies. Through integrated treatment, individuals learn to recognize that these conditions exist in relationship to one another and must be addressed together.

Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) has become an effective treatment plan for individuals dealing with both BPD and substance abuse. Through this approach, individuals learn specific skills to manage distress, tolerate stress, and build more effective relationships.

Christian counselors often integrate faith-based perspectives and evidence-based treatments to help clients understand their value in Christ as they develop practical tools to manage symptoms. This process involves learning that emotions do not have to be escaped or numbed. Even intense emotions can be experienced, understood, and regulated in healthy ways.

Finding the Support You Need

The relationship between BPD and substance abuse is a reflection of a human tendency to seek relief from pain through whatever feels available. For treatment to be effective, individuals must understand the different patterns of BPD and how they intersect with addiction.

Each type of BPD – the discouraged, the impulsive, the petulant, or the self-destructive – presents a unique challenge and strength in the recovery process. The consistency is the need for integrated treatment that addresses both the emotional dysregulation involved with BPD and addictive patterns.

Healthy recovery includes building new skills, developing healthier coping mechanisms, and discovering that lasting peace isn’t found by escaping emotions. Instead, you can learn to navigate feelings with grace, support, and God’s Word.

If you or someone you know is facing the complex challenges of BPD and substance abuse, professional support can make a meaningful difference in your recovery. Christian counselors are trained to integrate faith-based encouragement with evidence-based treatment to help you navigate this journey and find lasting recovery.
